description: Richard's broken promises, the decline of serfdom and the long shadow of 1381 on English politics.
content_html:
Was 1381 a Failure or a Beginning?

At first glance, the Peasants’ Revolt of 1381 looks like a comprehensive failure. The rebels were defeated, their leader killed, their charters revoked. Hundreds were executed in the reprisals that followed. Serfdom was not abolished. The Poll Tax, though withdrawn, was replaced by other forms of taxation. Yet historians have argued that the revolt’s long-term significance was profound — that it marked a turning point in the relationship between rulers and ruled, even if the immediate results were suppression and disappointment.

Richard’s Broken Promises

Almost immediately after the revolt was crushed, Richard II withdrew every concession he had made at Mile End. The Mile End charters were cancelled. Peasants who had believed their freedom was secured returned to find nothing had changed legally. Richard’s reported words — whether or not he used exactly these — that “villeins you are and villeins you shall remain” captured the ruling class’s collective determination to restore the pre-revolt order.

Parliament also revoked any concessions made under duress, and the Poll Tax was never levied again in this form — one concrete and lasting concession. But the broader legal framework of serfdom remained intact in law, even if it was being eroded in practice.

Key Fact

The immediate aftermath: the Poll Tax was never levied again; all the Mile End charters were revoked; serfdom remained legal; hundreds of rebels were executed. The revolt achieved only one immediate concrete gain — the abandonment of the Poll Tax — but its longer-term significance was much greater.

The Decline of Serfdom

Although serfdom was not legally abolished in 1381, it continued to decline steadily over the following century. The revolt had demonstrated, dramatically, that the peasantry would resist when pushed too far. Lords who might have considered reasserting their rights by force after the revolt faced a less cooperative and more assertive peasantry. The practical economics of the post-plague labour market continued to work against serfdom: it remained more economical for most lords to convert labour obligations to money rents than to try to enforce them.

By the mid-fifteenth century, the decline of serfdom was well advanced across much of England, though it was never abolished by a single act of Parliament. Historians debate the precise role the revolt played in this process: some argue it accelerated the pace of change; others that the economic forces set in motion by the Black Death would have produced the same outcome regardless. The consensus is that 1381 was one significant factor in a long structural change.

Despite the violent suppression of 1381, the peasantry did not retreat into passivity. The revolt had demonstrated that collective action was possible — that ordinary people could march on London, force a king to negotiate and make the ruling class fear for its position. This assertiveness did not evaporate. Local resistance to labour obligations continued across England throughout the later fourteenth and fifteenth centuries. The revolt’s memory became part of a broader tradition of popular protest in English history.

Control of Wages After 1381

Parliament continued to attempt to control wages after 1381, passing further legislation in line with the original Statute of Labourers. But the practical effectiveness of wage controls diminished. The labour shortage that the Black Death had created persisted well into the fifteenth century, and the economic forces pushing wages up were simply stronger than the law could overcome. By the early fifteenth century, real wages for agricultural workers were higher than they had been before the Black Death — a quiet economic victory that had been fought for in the fields, on the roads to London, and at Smithfield.

Key Fact

The revolt’s long-term significance: the Poll Tax was abandoned; serfdom declined gradually over the following century; real wages rose; and the revolt demonstrated that the peasantry would resist political exploitation — a lesson that shaped how subsequent rulers calculated what they could demand from their subjects.

Effects on the Hundred Years’ War

The revolt had direct consequences for England’s conduct of the Hundred Years’ War. The years around 1381 marked a period of significant English military setback in France, as Charles V’s campaigns had recovered much of the territory won by Edward III and the Black Prince. The fiscal crisis that had produced the Poll Tax — the need to fund a failing war — had contributed directly to revolt at home.

After 1381, the government was far more cautious about imposing heavy direct taxation, particularly on the poorest. This constrained the resources available for military campaigns in France. The revolt thus indirectly reduced the financial pressure that could be put on the poorest for war — not because the ruling class had become more sympathetic, but because they had learned that there were limits to what they could extract.

The revolt also marked a significant moment in the history of political consciousness in England. The rebels articulated specific demands — the abolition of serfdom, freedom to trade, equality before the law — in a context where ordinary people did not have formal political representation. The act of marching to London, forcing the king to negotiate and articulating a programme of reform was itself significant, regardless of the immediate outcome. Historians who see the revolt as part of a long tradition of popular politics in England often point to 1381 as a foundational moment.
exam_tip_html: On “explain significance” questions about the Peasants’ Revolt, you must address both significance at the time AND significance over time. At the time: immediate defeat, revocation of all promises, executions. Over time: the Poll Tax was abandoned; serfdom declined; wages rose; the revolt shaped future rulers’ calculations about taxation. Do not fall into the trap of saying the revolt “failed completely” — that misses the long-term picture. For the “how far” extended question, always structure your argument with clear points for, against and a substantiated final judgement.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Immediately after the revolt, Richard II revoked all promises made at Mile End; serfdom remained legal; hundreds of rebels were executed; the only concrete gain was the permanent abandonment of the Poll Tax.
  • In the longer term, serfdom declined steadily over the following century, driven by economic forces and persistent peasant resistance rather than any single law; real wages rose and the assertiveness shown in 1381 continued to shape popular politics.
  • The revolt constrained future royal fiscal demands on the poorest, indirectly affecting the funding of the Hundred Years’ War; its political significance lay in demonstrating that ordinary people could force the king to negotiate and that rulers faced limits on what they could extract.

practice_questions.text: Describe one immediate consequence of the failure of the Peasants' Revolt in 1381.
practice_questions.marks: Award up to 2 marks: 1 for a simple identification, 2 for a developed feature. Example: Richard II revoked all the charters granted at Mile End [1]; peasants who had believed their freedom was secured returned to find serfdom still legally intact and the promises of abolition cancelled [1].

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the decline of serfdom in England after 1381.
practice_questions.marks: Award 2 marks per feature. Feature 1: Although serfdom was not legally abolished, it declined steadily over the century following the revolt [1]; most lords found it more practical to convert labour obligations to money rents than to enforce them against an assertive, post-plague peasantry [1]. Feature 2: The revolt had demonstrated that the peasantry would resist when pushed too far [1]; this changed how lords calculated the risks of reasserting their rights, contributing to a more cautious approach to serfdom enforcement [1].

practice_questions.text: Explain one consequence of the Peasants' Revolt for the Hundred Years' War.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Explains a consequence in depth — the government's caution about heavy direct taxation after 1381 constrained resources available for French campaigns; or the revolt had been partly caused by the costs of a failing war, demonstrating the connection between foreign policy and domestic stability. Secure: Explains a consequence with relevant factual support. Developing: States a consequence with limited development. Emerging: Vague point without factual detail.

practice_questions.text: Explain one reason why the Poll Tax was a more significant concession than it appeared at the time.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Identifies the significance — the Poll Tax was never levied in this form again; it showed that popular resistance could force a retreat by the government on fiscal policy; it set a precedent that direct flat-rate taxation was politically dangerous. Explains this in depth with precise factual knowledge. Secure: Identifies the significance with relevant factual support. Developing: States a point with limited explanation. Emerging: Vague reference without specific factual detail.

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of the Peasants' Revolt of 1381 in the history of England.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Explains significance at the time (immediate defeat, executions, revocation of promises, but Poll Tax abandoned) and over time (gradual decline of serfdom; rising real wages; rulers more cautious about extreme taxation; revolt as a founding moment in popular political tradition). Precise factual knowledge throughout. Secure: Explains significance at the time with some longer-term reference. Developing: Describes the revolt without clearly explaining significance. Emerging: Limited knowledge; significance not addressed.

practice_questions.text:
'The Peasants' Revolt of 1381 was a failure because it did not achieve its immediate aims.' How far do you agree?
Use your own knowledge to support your answer.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Agrees and disagrees with precise factual knowledge. Agrees: the Mile End charters were all revoked; serfdom was not abolished; hundreds were executed; John Ball was killed. Disagrees: the Poll Tax was permanently abandoned; serfdom declined over the following century; wages rose; the revolt demonstrated that rulers faced limits on what they could demand; it shaped the political consciousness of ordinary people. Reaches a substantiated overall judgement about whether short-term failure equals long-term failure. Secure: Makes points for and against with evidence. Developing: Describes outcomes without evaluating the interpretation. Emerging: Simple response; no judgement.

knowledge_checks.q: Which was the one concrete and lasting concession won by the Peasants' Revolt of 1381?
options: The right to free trade for all peasants
The permanent abandonment of the Poll Tax

knowledge_checks.q: What happened to the charters granted by Richard II at Mile End?
options: They were implemented and serfdom was gradually abolished
They were revoked after the revolt was suppressed
They were passed to Parliament for debate
They were lost and their contents are unknown

knowledge_checks.q: Although serfdom was not abolished by law in 1381, it _____ gradually over the following century as lords converted labour dues to money rents.
The revolt's effects on the Hundred Years' War included making the government more cautious about heavy _____ on the poorest subjects to fund military campaigns.
Match each outcome of the Peasants' Revolt to whether it was immediate or long-term:
right: Long-term: gradual process over the following century
Immediate: happened within weeks of the revolt's end
Immediate: all promises withdrawn after revolt suppressed

flashcard_questions.q: What was the one concrete lasting gain from the Peasants' Revolt of 1381?
flashcard_questions.a: The Poll Tax was permanently abandoned and never levied in that form again.

flashcard_questions.q: What happened to the Mile End charters after the revolt was suppressed?
flashcard_questions.a: They were all revoked — Richard II withdrew every promise.

flashcard_questions.q: What was the long-term fate of serfdom in England after 1381?
flashcard_questions.a: It declined gradually over the following century, though never abolished by a single law.

flashcard_questions.q: Why did serfdom continue to decline even after the revolt failed?
flashcard_questions.a: Economic forces from the labour shortage meant lords found it more practical to accept money rents than enforce labour dues.

flashcard_questions.q: How did the revolt affect future royal taxation on the poorest?
flashcard_questions.a: The government became more cautious about heavy direct flat-rate taxes, constrained by the memory of 1381.

flashcard_questions.q: What did the revolt demonstrate about the political consciousness of ordinary people?
flashcard_questions.a: That they could organise, march on London, force a king to negotiate, and articulate a programme of reform.

flashcard_questions.q: How did the revolt affect England's conduct of the Hundred Years' War?
flashcard_questions.a: Caution about taxation constrained resources for French campaigns; the war had partly caused the revolt in the first place.

flashcard_questions.q: What were real wages for agricultural workers like by the early fifteenth century compared to before the Black Death?
flashcard_questions.a: Higher — the sustained labour shortage eventually produced real wage gains despite legal opposition.

flashcard_questions.q: What did Richard II reportedly say when pressed to honour his promises after the revolt?
flashcard_questions.a: Attributed words: 'Villeins you are and villeins you shall remain' — though the exact wording is disputed.

flashcard_questions.q: By the mid-fifteenth century, how advanced was the decline of serfdom in England?
flashcard_questions.a: Well advanced across much of England, though it was never abolished by a single Act of Parliament.

flashcard_questions.q: How many rebels were approximately killed in the reprisals following the Peasants' Revolt?
flashcard_questions.a: Historians estimate several hundred, though precise figures are uncertain.

flashcard_questions.q: Name one way the Peasants' Revolt's memory influenced English political history.
flashcard_questions.a: It became part of a tradition of popular protest; the name 'Poll Tax' remained politically toxic for centuries.

glossary_terms.definition: The charters drawn up at Mile End on 14 June 1381, promising abolition of serfdom and other concessions; all revoked by Richard II after the revolt was suppressed.
Tax that was abandoned after the Peasants' Revolt of 1381 because of widespread resistance; its abolition was a rare immediate concession to rebel demands.

The gradual disappearance of legal serfdom in England over the century following the Black Death and the Peasants' Revolt, driven by economic changes and peasant resistance rather than any single legal act.
